activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: VisiCalc, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston and released for the Apple II in 1979, was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers.
story:
Grace's mother's office smelled like burnt coffee, and the desk lamp flickered because the building was old and kind of dilapidated, with wires nobody had fixed since the eighties. Grace sat at her mother's spare chair with a practice spreadsheet open on the screen. She had a real reason to learn this: she was tracking her dog-walking money, six neighbors so far, and she wanted a chart to show her mother that her business deserved a raise in her allowance.

Thorin had come along because his own mother worked two floors up, and he wanted to print a poster for the school amendment to the robotics club rules, the one that would let sixth graders join. He leaned over Grace's shoulder. "You could just add it up on paper," he said.

"Thirty-two walks, Thorin. On paper." She typed =SUM(B2:B7) into the cell, pressed Enter, and the total appeared: one hundred forty dollars. It felt slightly like magic. Then she highlighted the column, clicked the bar chart button, and six bars grew on the screen next to her numbers. The third bar, for Mrs. Delgado's enormous sheepdog, towered over all the others.

That was when it stopped looking right to her. The chart said Mrs. Delgado paid the most, which was true, but the totals didn't match what Grace had in her notebook. Twenty dollars were missing. She stared at the bars, then at the numbers, then clicked on the formula cell. =SUM(B2:B7). Row eight was empty, but row nine held her first week's payment from the Hendersons, twenty dollars, which she had typed below everything else by accident. The formula couldn't see it. The bars were honest; her setup was wrong. She typed =SUM(B2:B8) instead, and the total jumped and a seventh bar sprang up beside the sheepdog's.

Her mother's colleague, an older man named Mr. Ong who kept paper clips in a drawer older than Grace, stopped by and watched the bars re-sort themselves. "You know, my brother-in-law did the same thing on the first home spreadsheet," he said. "VisiCalc, it was called. Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston wrote it, and it came out for the Apple II in 1979. He showed me on his machine, typing little sums."

"Wait, it was that old?" Grace asked.

"Nineteen seventy-nine. Before you, before me at this job." He tapped the screen gently. "Same idea, though. You change a number, everything changes."

Thorin had stopped printing his poster. "Can you make my list do that? Everyone who signed the petition, by homeroom?" He slid his paper across the desk, and Grace saw her chance. "Only if you put my name on it as a supporter of the amendment." Thorin grinned and typed her name in himself.

Grace started a new sheet, entered homeroom names down column A, and counted the signatures into column B, checking each one twice.

"My bar's going to be the tall one," Thorin said, pointing at room twelve.

"Let's find out."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
story:
Jaxon had exactly four dollars, and the Malaysian food booth at the cultural festival had chicken satay for three fifty. The trouble was the other fifty cents. He wanted it for the raffle at the community table, where every ticket helped donate school supplies to families hit hard by the spring flood. The mayor had called those families impoverished at the assembly on Friday, and the word had stuck in Jaxon's head all weekend.

His friend Gus texted him from the parking lot: "Meet me at the Malaysian booth. My grandma is running it and she said we can help. Also there is SO much food." Jaxon read the message twice, pocketed his four dollars, and jogged past the drummers and the booths full of woven baskets to find Gus already tying on an apron.

Gus's grandmother pressed a plate of satay into Jaxon's hands and said something to Gus in Malay. "She says carry it to the table with your right hand," Gus translated. Jaxon looked down. Sure enough, she had placed the plate into his right palm, and when a man at the counter handed her money, he used his right hand too. Jaxon started watching. Every customer, every exchange, right hand. It was a pattern, and he wanted to know if it was a rule.

He tested it. When a woman reached for napkins, he held them out in his left hand, just to see. She paused, switched the napkins into her right hand, and smiled at him as if he were a small child who had dropped something. Gus leaned over. "In Malaysia, the right hand is for eating and for giving and getting things. It's respect. Grandma made me practice for a week before today." Jaxon filed that away and passed the next plate with his right hand, and Grandma nodded at him like he had passed a test.

The line grew long, and Jaxon worked the counter, right hand steady, learning to grab skewers and make change at the same time. His arm ached, but he noticed his left hand had adapted by holding the tray still while his right did everything else. At the end of the hour, Grandma pressed a wrapped bundle of satay into his hands, both of them this time, and refused his three dollars twice.

Jaxon ate his satay by the stage, then walked his whole four dollars to the community table. "Four tickets," he said, and slid the money across with his right hand. The volunteer grinned and dropped the tickets into his palm the same way.

"Good luck," she said. The drummers started up again, and Jaxon stood there holding his tickets like they were made of gold.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can help a person focus, such as before a test or a race.
story:
Joshua found Anabelle in the music room hallway, sitting on the floor with her violin case, staring at the wall. The recital was in forty minutes, and she looked like she wanted to be anywhere else on the planet. "I'm not going out there," she said. "My hands shake every time I think about it. That means it's too much anxiety. Right?"

Joshua sat down beside her. He had been thinking about this exact thing for a week, ever since the science test he'd been sure he would fail. His hands had shaken then, too, and his stomach had clenched, but when the paper landed on his desk his mind went sharp and quiet, and he'd finished with time to spare. Afterward he'd looked it up, because the shaking seemed to contradict the idea that nerves were always bad. The words on the screen said stress was the body's response to a demand or a challenge, and that short bursts of it could actually help a person focus, like before a test or a race. He hadn't believed it until he remembered the test.

"Give me your hand," he said. Anabelle held it out, palm up, and he watched it tremble slightly, like a leaf in a small wind. "Okay. Now tune your E string. Just that, nothing else." It was his test, his simple idea: if the nerves were pure poison, they should wreck everything equally. Anabelle frowned at him, then opened the case, set the bow, and drew the note. It came out clean and steady. Her shaking hand hadn't interfered at all. She tuned the A, then the D, and her shoulders came down an inch with every string.

"That's weird," she said. "I feel like a wreck, but I can still do this."

"That's the point," Joshua said. "The nerves are your body answering the challenge. Short burst. It's helping you focus, not breaking you." He grinned. "Probably don't try to feel like this all day, though. That part I can't fix."

"I have my own coping plan, thank you very much," Anabelle said, and stuck her tongue out at him, defiant even while sitting on the hallway floor. "Deep breaths. And I told my little brother there are boundaries, and his boundary is staying home tonight."

Ms. Clarke came around the corner with a clipboard, checking names. "Anabelle? You're third. Joshua, you're on stage crew, so get to the curtain rope." She walked on without stopping, her shoes clicking like a metronome.

Anabelle stood, snapped the case shut, and slung it over her shoulder. "If my hands shake out there," she said, "I'm going to pretend they're just keeping time." She pushed through the double doors into the warm noise of the auditorium, and Joshua ran for the curtain rope, which was made of some rough alloy wire that bit into his palms no matter how he gripped it. From the dark wings he watched her walk to the center of the stage, lift the violin, and breathe once.

The first note rang out clear into the rafters.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning is an ancient practice: the Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and for strangers.
story:
Aubrey had agreed to volunteer at the food bank that operated out of the recreation room at Maple Grove, the seniors' residence two blocks from her school, mostly because Annabel had promised there would be snacks. There were no snacks. There were forty boxes of donated groceries, a broken dolly, and a list of residents who couldn't come down to the front desk themselves. "So we bring the boxes up to them," said Annabel's grandmother, who ran the whole thing from a folding table. "Aubrey, you take the east wing."

The first three deliveries were easy. The fourth door belonged to a man who opened it exactly four inches, looked at the box of bruised apples and dented cans, and said, "I don't take charity." He tried to shut the door. Aubrey stuck her foot in it, which she regretted instantly, and said the first thing that came into her head: "It's not charity, it's... leftovers. It would just get thrown out." The door stopped. It opened maybe six more inches, which Aubrey decided to count as progress.

"Leftovers," the man repeated, as if testing the word. He took one apple, then, obstinately, the whole box, and mentioned something about a book. She couldn't get more out of him, so she went back to the folding table and asked Annabel's grandmother what he might have meant. Why would an old story make someone accept food they'd refused?

"Probably gleaning," Annabel's grandmother said. Aubrey must have looked blank, because she went on. "Gleaning is an ancient practice. The Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested, for the poor and for strangers."

Aubrey stood there turning that over. So the food was already set aside, on purpose, the way farmers left the edges of their fields. Nobody was doing anyone a favor. That was the rule underneath it. "So if I tell people the boxes are like the edges of the field," she said slowly, "it's not charity, it's how this is supposed to work?" She decided to test it. At the next door, a woman who had waved off a box last week, Aubrey said, "This is our gleaning box. The parts left over, for whoever needs them." The woman peered at her over her glasses. "Gleaning," she said. "My grandmother did that in Lithuania." She took the box and, unprompted, sent Aubrey back down with a jar of her late husband's antibiotic ointment, "in case anyone at that table has a paper cut."

By the end of the afternoon, Aubrey had delivered nine more boxes using the edges-of-the-field line, and only one person had refused, the original man's neighbor, who announced that she was allergic to apples, pears, and joy. On the way out, Aubrey meant to disclose her experiment to Annabel's grandmother but found she didn't have to. "Heard you found the magic word," the old woman said, sliding a granola bar across the folding table. Aubrey took it. Snacks after all.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Line dances, in which a group repeats the same set of steps facing the same direction, let people dance together without needing a partner.
story:
Claire spun in front of the store mirror for the third time, and the silver skirt flared out like a sparkler. "That's the one," said Brodie, hanging over the fitting room door with two more dresses over his arm. "Brodie, that's the one for somebody who can dance. I can't dance. I don't have a partner. I'm going to stand by the punch table all night like a raccoon at a campsite."

"You are not nocturnal, Claire. The dance is at seven." Brodie tossed her the blue dress anyway. "Also, half our grade doesn't have partners. Dakota doesn't. Neither does Mr. Khan's whole student council, and they call themselves the Decorations Guild like it's a secret society from a movie."

Claire pulled the blue dress on and frowned at herself. She had watched her older cousin at a wedding once, and the thing she remembered was a moment when nobody had a partner at all, and yet everyone danced together anyway. It had looked like rows of people, all facing the same way, doing the same steps over and over. "Wait," she said. "At my cousin's wedding, nobody was paired up, but everybody was dancing. They were all in lines. Like, all facing the same direction, doing the same little set of moves and then starting over."

Brodie blinked. "Electric slide," he said. "My mom does it at every barbecue."

Claire wanted to verify it, not just believe it, so she marched out of the fitting room in the blue dress, found the far corner by the sweater racks, and started a step pattern facing the wall. Step, touch, step, touch, turn. A cashier glanced over. A woman with a shopping basket smiled. Then a boy about their age, waiting bored outside a fitting room, drifted over and copied her from a few feet away, facing the same wall. "You just do the same steps?" he asked, doing them, clumsily and then less clumsily. "You don't need a girl to dance with?"

"You don't need anybody to dance with," Claire said, delighted. "You just need the few steps, and you're dancing with the whole line." Brodie joined in. The boy's little sister joined in. By the fourth repetition all four of them had it, stepping and touching and turning in a ragged, wonderful row between the racks of scarves.

Claire bought the silver skirt. "It moves when you do the turns," she told Brodie at the register. He grinned and pointed at the boy, who was still practicing by the sweeters, alone and completely happy. "See you at the dance," the boy called. "I'll be in the line."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens, the crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark.
story:
Piper held the strip of litmus paper over the first beaker and let one drop of liquid fall onto it. The paper turned pink. She wrote "vinegar, acid" in her lab notebook, then moved to the second beaker. One drop, and the strip went blue.

"Base," said Kenneth, reading over her shoulder. "That's the soap water, right?"

"It's supposed to be." Piper frowned at the third beaker, which Ms. Moose had labeled only with a question mark. "This one's the mystery. We have to figure out whether it's an acid or a base, and where it sits on the pH scale." The scale ran from zero to fourteen, with acids at the low end, bases at the high end, and seven in the middle. A mystery solution meant a mystery number, and Piper wanted to be the one to get it right before anyone else in the class.

She dipped a fresh strip into the question-mark beaker. Nothing happened. The paper stayed the same dusty purple it had been in the package. She tried a second strip, holding it under the surface for a full ten seconds while Edison counted. Still purple.

"That can't be right," Edison said. "Something's wrong with the paper."

Piper looked at the strip, then at the package on the counter. The label read "litmus paper," and under that, in smaller print, were the words she had skimmed past and not really read: made from litmus, a dye extracted from lichens. "Lichens," she said slowly, "are the crusty growths you find on rocks and tree bark." She thought about the gray patches on her grandmother's garden wall, the ones that felt like dry paint when you touched them. Someone had scraped things like that off a wall and turned them into the paper in her hand.

"So the paper isn't broken," Kenneth said. "Maybe the mystery liquid is right in the middle."

Piper checked the chart Ms. Moose had posted at the front of the lab. A solution that turned litmus neither pink nor blue sat at a pH of seven, which was neutral, neither acid nor base. She wrote "neutral, pH 7" in her notebook and carried the beaker up to Ms. Moose's desk to see if she had guessed correctly. Ms. Moose lifted the beaker to the window, swirled it once, and nodded.

On her way back to her station, Piper stopped at the window. There was a streak of pale green lichen on the outside of the glass, right at eye level, growing on the stone sill. "You turned into test paper," she told it.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Box breathing means breathing in for a count of four, holding for four, breathing out for four and holding for four, then repeating the pattern.
story:
The night before the overnight canoe trip, Justin lay on his bunk in Cabin 4 and listened to the loons out on the lake. His mind kept spinning through everything that could go wrong: capsizing, losing his paddle, getting sick in front of everyone. He had barely slept the last two nights, and Ms. Swampy had noticed him picking at his breakfast again. "You look wiped out," she'd said. He hadn't answered.

At lunch, Leanne slid her tray next to his. She was the only person at camp who seemed calm about the trip. "I saw you at the fire last night," she said. "You kept bouncing your knee. That's what I used to do before speeches."

Justin shrugged. "I just can't get my head to shut up."

"Same," Leanne said. She picked up her fork and drew an invisible square on the table, one slow side at a time. "Before my speech in April, my cousin taught me box breathing. It means breathing in for a count of four, holding for four, breathing out for four and holding for four, then repeating the pattern. Trace the square while you do it. Four sides, four counts each."

Justin tried it right there over his macaroni. In for four while his finger slid across the table, hold for four going down, out for four coming back, hold for four going up. His chest felt like it had unclenched a little, though he wasn't sure if that was real or just because he wanted it to be. Maybe it only worked for speeches. A canoe trip was a whole different problem.

That afternoon he decided to test it like a science experiment. He counted how many times his knee bounced during the hour before dinner on Tuesday: nineteen. Then he practiced the square five times before dinner on Wednesday, in the morning, at lunch, and lying in his bunk before lights out. Wednesday's count: seven. It wasn't zero, but it wasn't nineteen either. Something invisible was changing, and he could measure it.

He changed his mind about something else, too. He'd been staying up late whispering with Regan, thinking tiredness would make the night pass faster. But Regan mentioned that even a microbe gets messed up when its routine breaks, some fact from a documentary, and Justin figured if routines mattered that far down, they probably mattered for him. So he started going to bed at the same time every night, same square of breathing, no talking after.

Thursday morning, the canoes slid into the fog. Halfway across the lake, Justin's paddle slipped and sank, and for a second his chest went tight and his knee started to bounce. He traced the square on the gunwale, one side at a time, and by the time he finished, Regan had spotted the paddle floating behind them and turned the canoe around.

Ms. Swampy waved from the dock. "Justin! You look robust this morning."

"Got eight hours," he called back, and dipped his paddle again.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert are so dry that some weather stations there have never recorded rain.
story:
Camille unrolled the two graphs on the flat top of the trail marker and weighted the corners with pebbles before the wind could intervene. Roger leaned over her shoulder, and Jessy crouched on the other side, still holding the granola bar she'd been eating since the switchback.

"Rainforest first," Camille said, tapping the tall bars. "Look, every month has a stack of rainfall. Some of them go almost to the top of the page." The temperature line underneath wiggled but never dropped far, like a rope someone had laid almost straight. "Now the desert." She slid the second graph over.

Roger frowned. "Yours is broken. Half the bars are just gone."

"That's what I thought." Camille had spent half of Thursday evening redrawing it, sure she'd skipped columns by mistake. Then she'd counted them twice and found nothing missing. "But I counted. There's no February bar because there's no February rainfall to draw."

"So draw a zero bar," Roger said. "A little flat line, like the others."

Jessy shook her head slowly. "A zero bar means you measured zero. Missing means nobody ever measured anything at all." She pointed at the empty column. "It's not the same thing."

Camille looked down the trail, where Mr. Lindqvist was helping another hiker retie a boot. She pulled out the folded note he'd handed her at the trailhead that morning. "You said the answer's in the graphs themselves," she read aloud, "and in the note tucked inside your desert packet. Don't guess. Check." She dug through her pack, past the water bottle and the whistle, and pulled out a thin pamphlet about Chile. There, on the third page, was a sentence she'd skipped: parts of the Atacama Desert are so dry that some weather stations there have never recorded rain.

"Never," she said. "Not a little rain. Not some years and not others. Never."

"Notorious place for it, apparently," Jessy said, reading over her arm.

"So the missing bars are the data," Roger said slowly. "Blank is the fact."

Camille picked up her pencil. Instead of inventing bars, she wrote one word beside the empty columns: no record. Then she held the two graphs side by side, and the symmetry of the assignment struck her, one page crowded to the top, the other almost bare, and both telling the truth. "Mr. Lindqvist," she called down the trail, waving the desert graph overhead, "I think the gaps are supposed to be there."

He looked up, saw the empty columns, and gave her a thumbs-up before turning back to the boot.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Stress can show up in the body as headaches, a tight or upset stomach, sweaty palms or trouble falling asleep.
story:
Bentley was peeling an orange at the kitchen table when his stomach knotted again, the same squeezed feeling he'd had every Sunday night for three weeks. He put down the orange and pulled his notebook toward him. On the page he had written the dates of every stomachache, and next to each one, the word Monday.

"Are you keeping score of something?" his mother asked, drying a plate.

"Sort of," Bentley said. "It's a pattern. Sundays only." He stared at the list. Monday meant the tryouts for the school's knowledge team, where Ms. Boateng asked questions in front of everyone. He'd been practicing with Cedric all month, and Cedric wanted to be captain so badly he'd memorized two hundred facts about rivers. If Bentley's stomach kept acting up, Cedric would have to compete without him.

He found his phone and typed his symptoms into a search: stomach trouble only at night before something big. The words that came up surprised him. Stress can show up in the body as headaches, a tight or upset stomach, sweaty palms, or trouble falling asleep. He read it twice. That explained the headaches after studying, too, and why his palms had been slick the last two Sundays even though the kitchen was cool. It wasn't the oranges. His stomach was telling on his nerves.

Gurfateh had mentioned something like this once, so Bentley called him. "What do you do when your hands sweat before a test?"

"Box breathing," Gurfateh said. "Four counts in, hold four, out four, hold four. My uncle taught me. And I go to bed at the same time every night, even weekends, or I'm basically nocturnal and can't sleep when it matters."

Bentley decided to test it like an experiment. That night he set a fixed bedtime, left his river flashcards downstairs, and sat on his bedroom floor doing the slow counts until his shoulders dropped. When the tight feeling crept back, he counted again. He fell asleep before he finished the fifth round.

At tryouts on Monday, Ms. Boateng called his name second. His stomach twitched once, but his palms were dry, and he remembered the longest river in Asia on the first try. Cedric got captain, exactly as he'd hoped, and grabbed Bentley's arm on the way to their seats.

"You had the stamina for twelve rounds," Cedric said. "I thought you'd bail like last week."

"Almost did," Bentley said. "Ask me about my notebook sometime." He grinned and flipped his chair around to face the next question.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: A eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died; the word comes from Greek roots meaning to 'speak well of'.
story:
Florence sat on the porch steps of Grandma Ruth's house, holding three index cards she had filled and crossed out and filled again. After the funeral lunch, Auntie had leaned down and asked if Florence would say a few words at the memorial on Saturday, since she had been Grandma's garden helper every Saturday for three years. Florence had said yes before her brain caught up with her mouth. Now she had two days and no speech.

"Is that a eulogy?" Winnie asked, appearing with two paper cups of lemonade. She had come with her mother, who was inside helping fold napkins. "My grandpa's funeral had one. I looked it up after, because the word sounded like something you'd study in science. It comes from Greek, and it means to speak well of somebody." She handed Florence a cup. "So it's not a report. It's praise."

Speak well of. Florence turned that over. She couldn't list everything Grandma had done, like a book report on a person. She had to find one memory where Grandma was already at her best, and let it do the praising for her. She spread her cards on the step like a fan. The tomato summer. The hummingbird feeder. The time Grandma had taped a plastic prism to the kitchen window and rearranged the whole breakfast table so the morning light would land on it and scatter rainbows across everyone's toast, "because a rainbow improves an egg, Florence, everyone knows that."

Florence needed a test audience. She carried the cards to the living room, where her little cousin was hiding under a blanket fort because the grown-ups kept hugging him, and Winnie had draped a quilt over the back legs of the fort to insulate him from the sad, loud room. Florence crawled halfway in. "Pick one," she said, holding up the three cards. "Which story makes you think of Grandma being Grandma?"

He squinted at the cards, then at her. "The toast one. Tell the rainbow one." He pointed with a chicken leg he had smuggled from the lunch table, which was honestly very Grandma of him.

On Saturday, Florence stood at the front with the rainbow card. Her knees shook, but she kept her eyes on the prism hanging in the church window, throwing its own small colors on the floor, almost parallel to her feet. "My grandma believed a rainbow improves an egg," she began, and heard the first laugh come up from the room, warm and surprised, like the sun had just moved.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: In the United States, the national Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222, and it connects callers to a local poison control center at any hour.
story:
Rose had babysat exactly once before, and that had been for Melia's two cats, which mostly slept. Tonight she was watching Ms. Harper's little brother's toddler, a boy named Danny, while the adults were at a party down the street. Danny was notorious in the neighborhood for climbing things, and Rose kept him in view the whole time, which was why she noticed the exact moment the backyard went quiet.

Silence, she had learned from her tutor in math, usually meant something had gone wrong with a pattern. Danny had been banging a plastic truck against the fence, and then nothing. She found him by the back step, sitting in the grass with a spray bottle in his lap. The nozzle was off. A thin line of wet ran down his chin, and he was grinning at her the way toddlers grin when they know they have done something interesting.

Rose's stomach dropped. She scooped him up, held the bottle away from his grabbing hands, and squinted at the label in the fading light. Cleaner. Ordinary kitchen cleaner, but the words did not say much else. Her mother had once warned her that some cleaners could irritate skin just from contact, never mind swallowing. Rose could not tell whether Danny had actually sprayed any into his mouth, or only onto his shirt, and that not knowing was the worst part.

She carried him inside, digging for her phone. Last summer, in the safety unit her class had slogged through, Ms. Harper had made them memorize one number and had taped it to her own fridge as a demonstration. "Poison Help," she had said. "1-800-222-1222." Rose remembered chanting it with Raymond until it stuck, the way you memorize anything, by being annoyed enough to. She found the fridge, and there it was on a strip of tape beside a crayon drawing: 1-800-222-1222. She dialed with one hand while Danny chewed the collar of her jacket.

A calm voice answered on the second ring, even though it was past nine at night. "Poison Help, this connects you to your local poison control center," the woman said, as though it were noon. Rose described the bottle, the open nozzle, the wet chin. The woman asked questions slowly. What was on the label, all of it, even the small print. How long ago. Was he coughing, drooling, rubbing his eyes? Rose answered each one, her heart thudding, Danny's warm weight heavy against her arm.

They washed his face and hands at the sink, rinsed his mouth with water, and the woman stayed on the line while Rose checked the shirt. The wet turned out to be a squashed berry from the grass, purple, not cleaner at all. The nozzle had been off when Danny found it. "He gave you a scare," the woman said, and Rose laughed, a shaky sound.

Ms. Harper's brother's family came home at ten. Rose told the whole story, phone still in her hand, and showed them the taped number on the fridge. "It works any hour," she said. "Any hour at all." Outside the window, Danny pressed his purple-stained palm flat against the glass.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians check a diary against other sources, such as letters, newspapers and government records, to test whether its details are accurate.
story:
The diary lay open on the library table, its pages brown as old toast. Layla had found it in a box of facsimiles Mr. Bear kept at the back of his classroom, and she had claimed it fast, before anyone else could. Her assignment was to use one primary source to explain why settlers moved west in the 1800s, and a diary written by an actual settler seemed perfect. The writer, a woman named Esther Hale, described leaving Ohio in the spring of 1846 because her husband's crops had failed two years running and land in Oregon was said to be free for the taking.

"Free land," Layla murmured, copying the line into her notebook. "That's my answer."

Tia leaned over from the next seat. "Rylan would say you need more than one diary entry to justify a whole claim like that."

"Rylan's not here. He has a concussion from the soccer game, remember? He fell and hit his head on the goalpost."

"That's why he can't remember anything from last week," Tia said. "The doctor said no screens and no reading."

Layla turned the brittle page and stopped. Esther Hale had written, "We read in the St. Louis paper that the wagon trains will gather in April," and she had dated the entry March 3, 1846. But the copy of the newspaper clipping tucked into the same box, which Layla had almost skipped, was dated April 11, 1846, and it announced that the trains would gather in May. Her stomach did a small flip. One of them was wrong, and she did not know which.

She tried to be logical about it. If the newspaper was printed in April, Esther could not have read it in March, unless the newspaper's printed date was the mistake. Or Esther had written the wrong month, or the wrong year. Layla carried both documents to the school library and pulled the volume of government land records on the shelf Mr. Bear had marked for this project. In it she found Esther Hale's name on a claim filed in Oregon in 1847, which fit a departure in the spring of 1846, and, folded between the record's pages, a microfilmed letter from Esther to her sister dated February 27, 1846, saying, "We expect to read of the trains in the April paper."

The letter matched the newspaper and the record. The diary's March date was the odd one out. Layla wrote her findings in three neat columns, then underlined her conclusion: settlers moved west for free land, and Esther Hale really did go, proved by more than her own diary. Historians, she wrote at the bottom, check a diary against letters, newspapers and government records to test whether its details are accurate.

When Rylan came back to school with a bandage above his ear, she slid the notebook across his desk. "Guess which source lied to me."

Rylan squinted at the columns, then tapped the diary's date. "This one. It's the only one standing alone."

"March third," Layla said, and drew a slow, satisfying X through it.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The equality rights in section 15 of the Canadian Charter came into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws.
story:
Alex stood in the marble hallway of the courthouse with a photocopied page of the Canadian Charter clipped to his notebook. Mr. Quinn had given the class one task before the tour started: pick a right, any right, and be ready to explain it in their own words to a judge after lunch. Alex wanted section 15, the equality rights, because his grandfather had told him about a time when restaurants could exclude people just because of where their families came from. That seemed like a story worth telling.

Then Shanaya tapped his page. "Your sheet has a typo. It says the rights came into force in 1985. Chris's says the Charter came in 1982." She held up her copy. Hers matched Chris's. Alex squinted. At the bottom of section 15, in small print, stood the words "comes into force in 1985." Every other section had started three years earlier. He copied the page word for word into his notebook to make sure he wasn't misreading it, and it still said 1985. So it wasn't a typo, or all three photocopies were wrong the same way, which seemed unlikely.

"That makes no sense," Chris said, leaning over. "It's one document. How can one part start late?" Alex had a theory. Maybe the section was added later, like a patch on jeans. He tested it by checking the top of the page: section 15 was there in the original list, not stapled on. So his patch idea was wrong. While the rest of the class wandered toward the courtroom doors, Alex sat on the hallway bench and wrote a note on the back of his permission slip: "Mr. Quinn, my section started three years after the rest of the Charter. If it was in the document from the beginning, why the wait? Signed, Alex, who is now too curious to be lethargic about homework." He folded it and handed it to the tour guide, who said she would pass it along.

The morning courtroom session was about a dispute over a dental hygiene clinic that a town council had tried to shut down. The judge quoted the Charter twice. Alex listened hard, hoping equality rights would come up, but the case was about something else. His stomach growled through the whole thing, which Chris found hilarious.

At lunch, Mr. Quinn found Alex by the vending machines and held up the folded note. "Good question. I won't answer it, though. You're supposed to explain a right, not a date." He pointed to a thin book on the courthouse display table, a Charter handbook. "Try the index."

Alex flipped to section 15 and read the paragraph twice. The equality rights in section 15 had come into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws. So the section had been there all along, but the government had asked for those years first. Governments needed time to fix laws that treated people unequally. That wasn't a patch on jeans; it was more like giving the cook time before opening the restaurant. He scribbled it down in his own words, then wrote on the corner of the page, "Shanaya owes me a cookie for the typo comment."

Shanaya read it and handed over half a granola bar. "Close enough," she said. "Now go tell the judge before he leaves." Alex jogged down the hallway, notebook open, waving the page above his head.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks, so a bar or bat mitzvah student learns the chanted melody of their reading in advance from a printed book.
story:
Eva had memorized four verses of her Torah portion at Grandma's kitchen table, chanting them from a printed book with vowels, little dots and lines, plus the musical marks above the letters that told her which tune to use. Her bat mitzvah was in three weeks, and Grandma quizzed her every afternoon over tea. "Again," Grandma said, tapping the page when Eva stumbled on the third verse. "The melody has to live in you, not on the page."

At school, Annalise asked how it worked. "You just sing it, right?"

"I read it from my book," Eva said. "There's a whole system of marks."

Aubrey frowned. "So what happens at the synagogue? Do they hold the book up for you?"

Eva hadn't thought about that. She'd pictured herself at the reading desk with her practice book, following the dots and squiggles like sheet music. But she'd also seen photos of the Torah scroll, a long parchment rolled on two wooden handles, and she tried to remember seeing any marks in those photos. She couldn't. The letters had looked bare.

She tested it that Sunday. Grandpa drove her to the synagogue for rehearsal, and Mr. Lewandowski, the rabbi, unlocked the ark and unrolled the scroll to her portion. Eva leaned in. Rows of dark Hebrew letters marched across the parchment, and nothing else. No vowels. No tunes. Nothing above or below the letters at all.

"Where are the dots?" she asked.

"A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks," Mr. Lewandowski said. "You learn the chanting from your printed book, in advance."

Eva stared at the bare letters and felt like she was looking at a word puzzle with half the clues erased. So all those afternoons at Grandma's table, all the repetition until the melody lived in her, were not just practice. They were the whole point. The book would stay behind in her bag. In three weeks, only she would know the tune.

She went home and tried something new. She submerged the page under a stack of mail so she couldn't peek, then stood at the kitchen counter and chanted the third verse from memory. She got it right. She got the fourth verse right too, and the high note in the middle didn't wobble.

"You'd have been a plague to live with if you'd found this out the week before," Grandma said, pouring more tea.

"The week before it wouldn't have mattered," Eva said. "I'd have had time to panic and then fix it." She pulled the page out from under the mail and looked at the little marks one more time. "I don't even need you anymore."

She slid the book into her bag anyway, and chanted the verses for Grandma with her eyes closed.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: People with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms.
story:
Connor stood in the aisle of Kovalenko's Pharmacy with a list from his mother in one hand and a box of tissues in the other. Three days of fever had finally let go of him, but his legs still felt like they belonged to a sleepy emperor who refused to get off his couch. The list said cough syrup, tissues, orange juice, and soup, in his mother's handwriting, which was not ambiguous at all.

"Connor?" Annika was at the end of the aisle, holding a thermometer. "You had it too?"

"Since Saturday," he said. "I feel like a dishrag now, but a winning dishrag."

She groaned. "I got sick Monday morning. My mom sent me to get a thermometer because ours died." She looked at the boxes on the shelf as if one of them might accuse her.

Connor set the tissues in the basket and did some counting in his head. His fever had started Saturday afternoon. The sleepover at Colby's had been Friday night. Annika had been there, eating popcorn and beating everyone at the card game, completely fine. Or completely fine-looking.

"Wait," he said. "When did you start feeling sick?"

"Monday. Why?"

"Because I started feeling bad Saturday." He walked with her toward the cough syrup, thinking out loud. "If you gave it to me, you gave it to me Friday, when you seemed totally healthy. That means you were already contagious before you felt anything."

Annika frowned at the thermometer box. "That sounds unfair."

"It is unfair," Connor agreed. "But it also means nobody at the sleepover has to justify why they didn't stay home. You didn't know. There was nothing to know yet." He tested the idea against the facts again. "If people with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms, then Friday you were already passing it around, and Saturday I got it, and Monday you got knocked flat."

"Colby better not get it," Annika said. "His mom will send us a very long text."

Mr. Kovalenko appeared behind the counter as they carried their baskets up, glasses low on his nose. "Two flu customers in one afternoon. You two were at that sleepover, weren't you? Half the neighborhood has been in here." He rang up the syrup and the thermometer. "Wash your hands, drink your fluids, and no shared popcorn for a week."

Connor paid for the juice and soup with the money his mother had given him, counting the change carefully because his brain was still moving at half speed. Outside, the air was cold and clean, and the sidewalk outside the bakery smelled like cinnamon.

"I'm texting Colby," Annika said, already typing. "Telling him to watch for a fever and not to blame us, because we were healthy when it counted."

"Tell him to blame the flu," Connor said. "The flu is the villain here." He hoisted the bag onto his shoulder. "And tell him I want a rematch at that card game. When I'm not a dishrag."

Annika held up her phone, and on the screen Colby had already replied with a single word: "Sunday."

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A round-robin, in which each person speaks in turn around the circle, gives quieter members a guaranteed chance to share their ideas.
story:
Jayden spread the agenda across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with salt shakers. The Marsh Club had met three times already, and every meeting had gone the same way: he and Alma talked, Pyper said maybe two words, and nobody decided anything. This time he had a plan.

"Item one," he began when his friends pulled up chairs. "We budget our ten dollars for the cleanup trip to the estuary next Saturday. Gloves, trash bags, snacks. Item two, we pick our spot."

Alma launched in immediately. "Gloves are expensive. We should just wash our hands after."

"My mom has old garden gloves," Jayden said. "That saves four dollars right there."

Pyper sat with her hands folded, watching the salt shakers like they might tip over. Jayden remembered the last meeting, where she had opened her mouth twice and both times Alma had already moved on to something else. The problem wasn't that Pyper had no ideas. Something else was going on, and he wanted to test a hunch.

He held up a wooden spoon. "New rule for this part. We go around the circle, and every single person speaks in turn before anyone talks twice. It's called a round-robin." He pointed the spoon at himself. "I say gloves are covered, so my money goes to trash bags. Alma, you're next."

Alma frowned but went along. "Fine. I say we skip snacks and buy more bags."

The spoon moved to Pyper. She looked at it, then at the window, then at the map of the estuary spread under the salt shakers.

"We're choosing the wrong spot," she said quietly. "Everyone goes to the parking lot side because it's easy. But the tide pushes floating trash into the far bank where the creek curves. My grandpa fishes there and says it's full of plastic after a big tide." She traced the curve with one finger. "If we walk ten minutes along the trail, we'll collect way more."

The kitchen went silent except for the hum of the refrigerator.

"Item two, decided," Jayden said, grinning. He wrote far bank in capital letters and circled it twice. "Round-robin stays on the agenda. Item three: who's bringing the shovel for the stuck shopping cart?"

Pyper raised her hand, and this time she didn't wait for the spoon.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 33 of the Canadian Charter, the notwithstanding clause, lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights for up to five years, and the override can be renewed.
story:
Mya stood at the bottom of the city hall steps holding her notecards so tightly that the corners bent. Inside, the annual youth civics fair had taken over the marble lobby, and her display was supposed to explain one right from the Canadian Charter in her own words. She had chosen freedom of expression, mostly because it was easy. Now she wasn't so sure easy was good enough.

Last Sunday at her grandmother's house, the TV news had mentioned something called the notwithstanding clause, and her uncle and her father had argued about it until the potatoes went cold. Mya had sat quietly, listening. She'd caught enough to look it up later in the library's encyclopedia: Section 33 of the Charter let Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights for up to five years, and the override could be renewed. Five years, then five more. Rights that could be switched off like a classroom light, then switched off again. She'd written it on a card and slipped it into her pocket.

"You look like you're about to be eliminated in round one," said Xavier, appearing beside her with two paper cups of water from the fountain that never quite met anyone's standards of hygiene, its basin ringed with greenish stains. He handed her one anyway.

"It's too hot in there," she said, and it was true, the radiators clanking, the air smelling of floor wax and old paper. "Also I think my topic is wrong."

Ms. Mensah, a city councillor who judged the fair every year, stopped at Mya's table just after lunch. Mya gave her planned speech, then hesitated, then pulled the card from her pocket. "I picked freedom of expression because it was simple," she said. "But I read that Section 33 can override certain rights for up to five years, and it can be renewed after that. So the right exists, and then it can stop existing, and then it can stop existing again. That changed what I think my job is here."

Ms. Mensah tilted her head. "And what is your job?"

"To explain it in my own words, not just recite it. My dad thinks the clause is a safety valve. My uncle thinks it's a trap. I wanted to be objective, but I don't think I can be, because I have an opinion now." She turned her display board around. On the back, in marker still faintly smudged, she had written: "A right you can turn off is still a right, but you have to keep watching the switch."

Ms. Mensah read it twice. "Move your board so people see that side," she said. "And stand where the light from those windows hits it."

Mya flipped the board, wiped her damp palms on her skirt, and watched the afternoon sun pour across her words. Xavier gave her a thumbs-up from the fountain, and she squared her shoulders as the next visitor stopped at her table.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phishing is a scam in which someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away passwords or other private information.
story:
Jasmine held the phone box above her head like a trophy the moment her mom handed it over. "Rules first," her mom said. "Dinner table, chargers downstairs, and nothing you wouldn't show me." Jasmine agreed to all of it, even the last one, though she privately presumed her mom would forget that rule within a week. She spent the whole evening downloading her favorite game, adding Hallie and Salim by username, and setting a wallpaper of a red panda.

The next morning, while she was still brushing her teeth, the phone buzzed. A message from something called GameGuard Support read: "Your account will be deleted in 24 hours unless you verify your password. Reply now to keep your items." Jasmine's heart thumped. She had spent two years earning those items. Her thumb hovered over the keyboard, and she actually typed the first letter of her password before she stopped.

Something felt wrong. She had learned in school that real companies don't need your password, because they already have it on their own computers. If the game company was real, why would it ask? And why would an official message say "Reply now" like a stranger selling something? She had an idea for a test. She typed back, "Which email is on my account?" A real support person would know. The answer came instantly: "Just send password to confirm." No email. No name. Just the same demand, faster than any human could type it.

At school she showed the messages to Hallie at lunch. "That's called phishing," Hallie said, around half a sandwich. "My aunt fell for one last year and lost a whole month of photos." Salim leaned over, squinting. "I got that same text last week. I almost replied. I thought only gullible people fell for that stuff." He looked embarrassed, then grinned. "Good to know it just takes being tired and holding a new phone."

Jasmine blocked the number and reported it through the game's actual help page, where a real support person named her email back within an hour and confirmed her account was fine. She felt like she had passed some secret first test of phone ownership. That evening, she handed the phone to her mom at dinner without being asked. "New house rule?" her mom asked, raising an eyebrow. "Mine," Jasmine said, spearing a broccoli floret. "The phone is amazing, but it's not going to be a revolution in my life. I'm keeping the upper hand." Her mom laughed so hard she nearly knocked over the water glass.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Checking in privately afterward with a classmate who was teased, and telling them it was not okay, can help them feel less alone even if nobody stepped in at the time.
story:
The screen door banged shut behind Bennett, and the smell of Grandpa's kitchen rolled out to meet him, onions browning in a black skillet. Grandpa was quartering potatoes for a stew and explaining, as he always did, exactly what he was doing. "Potatoes are mostly carbohydrate," he said, "which is why they stick to your ribs." Bennett had brought his friend Madelynn along because her parents were working late, and Beau from his class had tagged along too, since Beau's grandmother lived two streets over.

Trouble started in the backyard, where Grandpa kept an old horseshoe pit. Madelynn's first toss went sideways and clattered into the fence, and Beau laughed. "You throw like a drunk flamingo," he said, and then he did it again, louder, a flamingo impression with flapping arms, and Madelynn's face went pink and she stared at her shoes. Bennett stood there holding a horseshoe, and his whole body felt like it had turned to cement. If he yelled at Beau, Beau would just get funnier to himself. If he told Madelynn it was fine, that would be a lie. So he said nothing, and after a minute Madelynn said she was going inside, and the game fell apart.

Bennett stayed out and pretended to practice his toss, but really he was turning the problem over. He thought about the time a kid got teased in math class and everybody laughed, and how the kid had seemed smaller for days afterward, like the laughing had kept echoing. He wondered about something he couldn't see directly: what actually made teasing stick to a person? Maybe it wasn't only the teasing itself. Maybe it was being alone in it, like being the only one who got rained on. He couldn't measure that, couldn't put a number on it, but he could test a hunch with an approximate experiment, the way Grandpa tasted stew and added salt without measuring.

He found Madelynn on the porch swing, sitting with her back to the yard. He sat down on the other end. For a second he thought about saying Beau hadn't meant it, but that wasn't true either, so he just said, "What he did out there wasn't okay. I should have said something, and I didn't, and I'm sorry."

Madelynn looked over at him. "You don't have to be sorry. You didn't do anything."

"That's kind of the problem," Bennett said. "I didn't do anything."

She almost smiled. "Flamingo arms, though. That was almost good."

"It was decent," Bennett admitted. "But the toss was better than the mocking. Want to go show Beau how it's done before the stew's ready?" Madelynn picked up a horseshoe from the rail and stood.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: No number of white swans can prove that all swans are white, but seeing a single black swan proves that claim false.
story:
The bean seeds had been sitting in their foam cups on the windowsill for nine days, and every one of Cyril's cups held nothing but damp soil. "This whole packet is dead," Cyril announced, tipping one cup so everyone at the lab table could see the plain black dirt. "Mine haven't sprouted, and the group next to us hasn't sprouted, and even Leslie's haven't sprouted. All the seeds in this packet are dead."

Levi stared at his own three cups. Leslie leaned over from the next table and shook her head. "My sister says no number of white swans can prove all swans are white," she said, "but one black swan proves that claim false. So nobody's sprouted yet. That doesn't prove anything." She tapped his cup. "Find one sprout and Cyril loses."

"But if they're not dead, why won't they grow?" Levi muttered. He touched the window glass. It was cold enough that his fingers ached, and when he breathed on it, a small fog bloomed and evaporated in seconds. The radiator was on the far wall, so no heat ever reached this side of the room. Mr. Demetriou had joked on Monday that the windowsill was basically tundra, and Levi had laughed, but now he wrote in his notebook: maybe the seeds aren't dead. Maybe the soil is too cold for sprouting. It was only a guess, though, and he underlined it twice to remind himself that a guess wasn't an answer until something tested it.

He raised his hand and asked if he could move one cup. Mr. Demetriou said sure, as long as he labeled it, so Levi carried a cup to the shelf above the radiator and taped a strip of paper to the side that said WARM, in handwriting that was honest but not what anyone would call eloquent. He watered the shelf cup and the windowsill cups with exactly the same amount from the same jug, because if the warm one sprouted and the cold ones didn't, he wanted it to be about the heat and nothing else. For two more days he checked every cup at the start of class, and every cup stayed empty, and Cyril grinned wider each time.

On the third morning Levi walked in, looked at the shelf, and stopped so fast that Leslie bumped into his backpack. A pale green hook was pushing up through the soil in the cup marked WARM, bent like a tiny question mark. Leslie grabbed his sleeve. "There," she said. "One black swan. Your seeds were alive the whole time." Levi carried the cup to Cyril's table and set it down in front of him without a word, then got his notebook and, next to his underlined guess, wrote in careful letters: supported.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: The hongi is a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand in which two people press their noses and foreheads together, symbolizing the sharing of the breath of life.
story:
The gurdwara parking lot was already full when Willow's mother dropped her off, so Willow carried the box of dates herself, careful not to step in the puddle by the steps. Inside, everyone removed their shoes and covered their heads, and Willow did the same, tucking her scarf the way she had learned at last year's open house. A woman at the door pressed her palms together and said, "Sat sri akal," and Willow said it back, even though she always felt she had to calibrate her pronunciation, slow on the first word and quicker on the second.

Her friends Hadi and Imran were already in the langar hall, sitting cross-legged on the floor mats. Beside them sat a boy she didn't recognize, with dark hair and a school jacket from a different school, and a girl who looked like his older sister.

"That's Wiremu," Imran whispered. "New. From New Zealand. His dad's the guest speaker tonight."

Willow set the dates near the serving tables, where volunteers were ladling dal into steel bowls. She had brought the dates because her grandmother always said you never arrive at someone's house or someone's holy place empty-handed, and she wondered if Wiremu's family had a rule like that too. They had. In front of Wiremu sat a paper bag of small green stones, and he was handing them out, one to each person who came near him.

"For the welcome," he said, giving one to Hadi. "We always bring something."

When Wiremu's father arrived, Willow watched him and Wiremu press their noses and foreheads together, gently, for a second. Then the father did the same with his daughter. Willow nudged Imran. "Did you see that?"

"Maybe it's only for family," Imran said.

That was the question Willow couldn't leave alone. If it was only for family, then the greeting was a closed door, and the stones were the open one. But she remembered her own grandmother, who kissed her on both cheeks but only shook hands with strangers, and Willow thought greetings could be doors that opened wider the longer you knew someone. She wanted to know which kind this was.

She calibrate-tested it the only way she could think of: she walked over, stood in front of Wiremu, and leaned in, pressing her nose and forehead against his for a brief second. He didn't pull back. He laughed.

"That's a hongi," he said. "It means we share the breath of life."

Imran tried it next, then Hadi, then two of the volunteers from the kitchen, and by the time the food was served, half the room had shared breath with Wiremu or his sister, and the other half were lining up. Willow sat back down on the mat and remembered the winter her class had a hamster, and how it had escaped and the whole grade seven hallway had organized a search party, and how a single small rodent had made twenty-six kids into a team in one afternoon. One small greeting seemed to be doing the same thing here.

The volunteers served dal and roti, and everyone ate with their right hand, which Hadi explained to Wiremu in a low voice while demonstrating. Willow watched Wiremu's sister tear her roti neatly with her left hand but eat with her right, and Willow thought that every house and every holy place had its own system of rules, learnable if you paid attention to what people's hands were doing. When the karah prasad came around in the steel bowl, Willow cupped both hands together to receive it, the way you were supposed to, and Wiremu copied her, and his sister nodded at him across the mats.

"These dates," Wiremu's father called out from across the hall, holding one up. "Who brought these?"

Willow raised her hand, and he pressed a date to his nose before eating it.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A spreadsheet cell's address is its column letter followed by its row number, so C4 is the cell in column C, row 4.
story:
Antoine sat cross-legged on Bodie's living room floor with a laptop balanced on a pillow, because Bodie's little sister had claimed the table for a puzzle. "The bake sale report is due to Ms. Rosen tomorrow morning," Antoine said. "She wants our cookie profits typed up, a total, and a bar chart. I've never made a spreadsheet in my life."

"Then you're learning today," Bodie said. "Type the sales in column B, one row per week." Antoine typed in the numbers, then stared at the empty box below them. Bodie leaned over. "In that cell, type equals, SUM, open paren, B1, colon, B7, close paren." Antoine typed it, hit enter, and the column added itself. "Okay, that's magic," he said, and even the puzzle-solving sister looked up.

The chart was harder. Antoine clicked here, dragged there, and the bars appeared crooked and gray. He tried to fix them, but he needed one more number, the total from his own notebook, which he had left at his residence down the street. He called Nina, who had copied his notebook numbers at school. Over the phone she said, "The week with the bake sale total? That's the one I wrote in the box on the second page, C4." Antoine hung up, then frowned at the screen. Nina was reading from her own notebook grid, not his spreadsheet. On his sheet, the letter came first and then the number, so the number he wanted had to live in a cell whose address meant column C, row 4. He tested his idea: he typed C4 into a blank cell, and the spreadsheet showed him exactly the bake sale figure. He'd found the rule. "Cells have street addresses," he announced. "Letter, then number. Like C4 means column C, row 4."

"Congratulations, you converted from confused spreadsheet guy to neighborhood data expert in one afternoon," Bodie said. Antoine laughed, dropped the correct number into the chart, and the bars snapped tall and blue. The biggest bar towered over the others, buoyant as a sail, because the bake sale week had earned almost double the rest.

Antoine saved the file twice, then emailed it to himself, then saved it on a flash drive, then saved the flash drive in his sock. "That's four backups," Bodie said. "Ms. Rosen is going to think you're hiding state secrets." Antoine pulled the flash drive out of his sock and held it up like a trophy. "This," he said, "is what sixteen dollars of cookie data looks like."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Each whole step on the pH scale is a tenfold change, so a solution at pH 3 is ten times more acidic than one at pH 4.
story:
Connor had inherited his grandfather's lab notebook, a fat green book full of careful measurements, and today he planned to add a page of his own. Ms. McKenzie had set out five unmarked cups on the long black counter: vinegar, lemon juice, soapy water, baking soda mixed with water, and one mystery liquid nobody could name. The task was to sort each cup as acid or base using nothing but strips of litmus paper.

He tore a strip from the little paper book and dipped it into the first cup. The paper turned pink, sharp and sudden as a struck match. "Acid," he wrote, and moved down the line. The strip in the soapy water flipped the other way, turning blue, and the smell of fake lemons drifted up from the cup beside it, sour enough to make his nose prickle.

Adelie slid over beside him, holding two of her own strips. "Look, vinegar is pH three and lemon juice is pH four," she said. "So vinegar's just a little more acidic. Barely a difference." She started to write "slightly more acidic" on her sheet.

"Wait." Connor frowned at the pH chart taped to the wall. Something about it snagged in his mind. He dipped fresh strips into both cups and laid them side by side on a paper towel, and the vinegar strip's pink was deeper, angrier, in a way that did not look little at all. He thought of his grandfather's notebook, how every entry tested an idea instead of guessing. "I don't think the scale works like that," he said slowly. "I think each whole step is a tenfold change. So pH three is ten times more acidic than pH four. It's not one step of difference, it's ten of them."

Adelie chewed her pen. "Ten times? From one number apart?" But she looked at the chart again, at the way the colors jumped, and crossed out what she had written. "Ten times," she echoed, writing it down.

Ms. McKenzie paused behind them on her way past the fume hood, where the leftover samples from the invasive knotweed experiment were drying on a rack. She glanced at their paper towel and gave a small nod, then kept walking. Adelie grinned and split their last strip in half, since the supply economy of the class meant each pair got only ten, and handed Connor the spare piece for the mystery cup.

Connor dipped it, and the paper turned a pink so deep it was almost red.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects.
story:
The fire station smelled like rubber boots and old coffee, and Ryan stood in the back of the group wondering why he had even raised his hand to come. Joey had begged him, the way he always did, and Ryan had said yes the way he always did, and now here he was staring at a display case while Ms. Nasser counted heads.

The case held things from the station's past: a leather bucket with a long crack down its side, a folded paper roster gone brown at the edges, and a painting of a horse-drawn engine. A small dial sat inside the case with two needles, and Ryan leaned close. One needle had a tiny label that read "humidity." As he watched, it crept upward, then slowly back down.

"Joey," he whispered, tugging his friend's sleeve. "Look at this. The needle moves when the big bay door opens."

Joey shrugged. "It's a thermometer, probably."

Ryan didn't think so. A thermometer would jump when the door let in cold air, and this one moved even when nobody stood near it. He decided to test it. He watched the needle, waited until Ms. Nasser called Samson over to look at the pole slide, then asked the station's tour guide, "What's that dial for?"

"Fire stations like ours keep a little museum corner," the guide said. "Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects. See the bucket? That crack happened before we started controlling the case."

Ryan looked at the bucket again, the split running like a dry riverbed through the leather. So it wasn't age alone. It was the air itself, swelling the wood, shrinking it, swelling it again, a hundred small pulls until something gave. He thought about the warped door in his grandmother's house, the one his dad said he would inherit someday along with everything else in it. All those years, everyone blamed the door. Maybe the door had never had a chance.

Samson pressed his nose to the case. "The painting's got green stuff on the hill."

"Lichen," the guide said. "It grows on rocks and trees, slow as anything. That painter put it there on purpose."

Outside, the afternoon sky had gone the color of a struck match, luminous behind the tower where the brass pole rose. Ryan remembered last fall, when Joey had wanted him to try out for soccer and he'd said no because he was afraid of being bad at it, and how the whole season had gone by without either of them mentioning it again. He still didn't know if saying no had been smart or just safe.

The bay door rumbled open for a returning engine, and the needle inside the case began, slowly, to climb.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: Copying =SUM(B2:B10) one column to the right turns it into =SUM(C2:C10), because ordinary cell references are relative and shift with the formula.
story:
The bell on the door of Fortin's Phone Fix rang twice before ten, which meant the Saturday rush was coming. Katherine had been drafted because her mother was friends with Ms. Fortin, and because, as Ms. Fortin put it, "You're thirteen, you know computers." Katherine had not argued. She got to sit behind the counter with the shop's ancient laptop and a mug of hot chocolate, which was better than laundry.

"Here's the job," Ms. Fortin said, sliding a paper across the counter. "Every repair this week, day by day. I need totals and a bar chart, because the accountant says my receipts look like a tsunami hit them." She pointed at column B, Monday's charges. "Add those."

Katherine typed into B11: =SUM(B2:B10). The total appeared, forty-one cells of chaos reduced to one number. She sat back, satisfied, and then did the math on the rest of the week. Five more days. Five more columns. She was going to be here until noon.

Rory, who supervised the front counter on Saturdays and wanted very badly to be promoted to "senior counter associate," leaned over. "You could just type it five more times."

"I could also walk to school on my hands." Katherine stared at B11. The formula said B2:B10. Column C held Tuesday. If she copied the formula one column to the right, what would it say? She had a theory, and theories were free. She copied it, clicked C11, and pasted. C11 read =SUM(C2:C10). Not B2:B10 again. The references had moved with it.

"Oh," she said quietly.

"Oh what?" said Rory.

She dragged the little square at the corner of C11 straight across to G11, and one by one every column total filled itself in. Wednesday. Thursday. Friday. Saturday. Rory made a small sound, like a kettle deciding whether to whistle.

"It's the same formula," Katherine said. "Well, an equivalent one. It shifts."

"Show me that again," Rory said. "Slowly. If Ms. Fortin sees I can do that, she has to make me senior counter associate. There's no counter associate union, but there should be."

Katherine highlighted the totals, clicked the bar chart button, and a chart sprang up, six fat bars leaning sideways like commuters on a train. Ms. Fortin came out of the back, looked at it, and looked at it some more.

"Saturday's the tall one," she said. "Which is strange, because we're closed Saturdays."

Rory and Katherine turned to the chart together.

"Rory," said Ms. Fortin, "what exactly have you been doing here on Saturdays?"

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Watering deeply and less often encourages roots to grow downward, while frequent light sprinkling keeps roots near the surface where soil dries fastest.
story:
Lily claimed the back corner of the yard on the first Saturday of spring break, and by lunchtime she had dug two beds, one for tomatoes and one for carrots, with a fence of sticks around them to keep out the dog. "Welcome to the Tomato Growers' Guild," she announced, pinning a paper sign to the fence. "Membership: me."

"Can I join the guild if I only like eating tomatoes?" asked Briella, who had come over to watch and, Lily suspected, to steal the good chair.

"Membership fee is one watering can," Lily said, and Briella ran home to get one.

Their watering routines became a joke between them. Lily soaked her tomato bed once a week until the soil was dark and heavy, then left it alone. Briella, who liked any excuse to be outside, sprinkled the carrots lightly every single afternoon, flicking water around like a chef seasoning fries. "A little drink for the little plants," she declared, and Lily rolled her eyes and let it go.

For three weeks both beds looked happy. Then came the hot week, seven days of sun that made the patio too bright to look at. Briella's carrots drooped first, every single morning, like a row of fainting pencils. Lily's tomatoes sagged a little at noon and stood back up by evening. Lily stood between the beds with her hands on her hips, thinking.

She decided to excavate. With the trowel she dug carefully beside one drooping carrot, then beside one steady tomato, following the roots down with her finger. The carrot's roots were shallow, huddled near the top of the soil, exactly where the sun baked everything dry by midmorning. The tomato's roots ran deep into dark, cool ground.

"Briella, your carrots are lazy," Lily called across the fence. "You've been spoiling them. All that daily sprinkling kept their roots near the surface, where the soil dries fastest. Mine had to go hunting for water, so they grew downward."

"So deep watering less often makes tough roots," Briella said slowly, "and my way makes little spoiled surface babies."

"Exactly. You've been running a carrot spa."

Briella switched to Lily's method, one deep soak and then patience, even though patience was not her best subject. By the end of August the carrots stood straight through the heat, and the guild sign had two names on it, the second written in purple marker. Mr. Demetriou leaned over the fence to admire the tomatoes, calling the setup "very sophisticated for a couple of twelve-year-olds," and Lily handed him the first ripe one, warm from the sun.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Apps must ask permission to use a phone's camera, microphone or contacts, and you can take that permission away later in the phone's settings.
story:
Evan sat on the edge of his bed with the new phone warm in his hands, the family group chat already blinking with messages. "Welcome to the twenty-first century," his mom had typed, followed by his grandmother's thumbs-up, which she sent to everything. He had wanted this phone since September, when Valeria and Aubrey had made a video for the science fair and he'd only been able to stand behind the camera, borrowing his mom's old tablet that died if you looked at it wrong.

He typed "thanks everybody" and then started downloading apps. A flashlight app came up first, free, with a million downloads. He tapped Install, and a box popped onto the screen: the app wanted permission to use his contacts. Evan stopped, thumb hovering. His whole address book, for a light. He thought about the group chat, about Gran's number, about Valeria's address sitting in there from when they'd planned that project. He closed the box, and the app worked anyway, a plain white beam across his dark ceiling.

Still, the message nagged at him. In his last class of the year, Mr. Halvorsen had said something Evan had half ignored at the time, something about how apps must ask permission to use a phone's camera, microphone or contacts. What Evan hadn't known, until he dug around in the phone's settings that evening, was that you could take that permission away later. He found a list of every app and what it was allowed to touch. The video app he'd installed had the camera and the microphone, which made sense. A weather app had his location. He scrolled slowly, checking each one like he was counting his own money.

"What are you doing?" Valeria texted. "Aren't you playing the basketball game yet?"

"Checking permissions," he wrote back. "Did you know you can shut them off in settings?"

"Wait, really? My flashlight app has ALL my contacts. It had them for like a year."

She went quiet, and he pictured her in her kitchen with the same screen in front of her, scrolling. He remembered the science fair again, how he'd let Aubrey post their video without reading what the app asked for, and how he'd felt afterward like he'd signed something without looking. He couldn't decide if that had been careless or just thirteen. Maybe both. The app store page had called the developer "a prestigious software company," which had reassured him at the time and didn't now. Prestigious companies still ask for your contacts to turn on a light.

In the group chat, his grandmother sent another thumbs-up, and beneath it he typed: "Gran, do me a favor. Check your settings tonight. I'll show you how tomorrow."

"Show me what?" she replied.
