He picked up the phone and started walking to the kitchen. "I'll show you when I get there," he called out loud, since she was only down the hall.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Lunar New Year, celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere, falls on a new moon between January 21 and February 20.
story:
Camille had circled February 10 on the calendar in red marker, because that was the day of last year's Lunar New Year dinner at Grandma's, and she wanted the class project to match. Archer and Yasser were counting on her. The assignment was to record a family tradition on video, and she had promised them dumplings, red envelopes, and her grandmother's lanterns. When she asked her mother to confirm the date, her mother laughed and said, "It's not February 10 this year. It moves." Camille stared at the calendar. Holidays did not move. Her birthday never moved.

She called Yasser from the kitchen. "Ask your family when Tet is," she said, because Yasser's family also kept Lunar New Year, only they called it Tet. He called back ten minutes later. "January 29." Different again. Archer, whose family did not celebrate it at all, texted a screenshot of something he had found: Lunar New Year, celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere, falls on a new moon between January 21 and February 20. Camille read it twice. A new moon. She looked out the window at the darkening sky, then at her calendar, and flipped back through the months. The date could land anywhere inside that month-long window, so of course it jumped around.

At Grandma's house two days later, the kitchen smelled like ginger and fried scallions. Camille helped fold dumplings at the counter, pressing the edges with a fork the diligent way her grandmother had taught her, every crimp tight so the filling would not leak. She asked whether Grandma had a calendar somewhere. Grandma wiped her hands and pulled a small booklet from a drawer, printed with moon phases. "We follow the moon," she said. Camille traced the little circles with her fingertip. Dark, then a sliver, then full, then dark again. The new moon, she thought, was the day the circle went black.

She wanted to test it. She texted Yasser: "Look up the new moon for January 29." He wrote back that it matched. Then she found this year's date for the dinner, February 17, and checked that too, hiding her phone under the table so Grandma would not think she was being rude. New moon again. Her idea held. The moving dates were not random; they were a pattern you could not see by looking at a wall calendar at all, because the wall calendar did not track the moon.

Grandma handed her a red envelope and then a plate to conserve, meaning carry it carefully to the dining room without spilling. At the table, Camille told everyone the plan for the video, and Grandma pointed at the painting above the cupboard, horses and mountains from a dynasty long ago, and said they could film that too, since it had come down through the family. On Saturday, Archer and Yasser arrived with the camera, and Camille stood in the doorway holding the booklet of moons.

"Start on this," she said, and held it open to the page where the circle went dark.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
story:
Beatrice had forty-two dollars in her pocket, and the star pin at the kiosk by the fountain cost forty. It was a small enamel comet with a tail of real glitter, and there were only twelve of them, according to the sign. The line in front of the kiosk stretched past the pretzel stand. Oceane was already near the front, waving.

"You got here fast," Beatrice said, squeezing in beside her.

"I've been here since the mall opened," Oceane said. "Last month these pins were fifteen dollars. Then the singer wore one, and now everybody wants one, and there aren't many, so the price went up. My brother says that's just how it works."

Andres appeared with a pretzel and a bottle of water. He held both up like evidence. "You know what's weird? This water cost a dollar. It keeps me alive. And yesterday my aunt's ring got appraised at the jewelry store upstairs, and a diamond the size of a crumb is worth thousands." He took a bite. "In this old book, The Wealth of Nations, from 1776, this guy Adam Smith wrote that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal. He noticed it almost two hundred and fifty years ago."

"Because there's water everywhere," Beatrice said slowly, "and diamonds almost nowhere." She looked at the line, then at the price sign. "So if the pins really are everywhere somewhere, the price should fall." She had an idea, and it felt like a piston firing in her brain, one clean push of motion.

She left the line. Behind the kiosk, past the storage door marked with a plastic plant that had somehow grown invasive across the whole wall, Beatrice saw stacked boxes. She asked the cashier, who was restocking, "How many of those comet pins do you actually have?" The cashier laughed. "Six boxes. Two hundred pins. The twelve is what fits on the display." Beatrice walked back to Oceane and told her. "They're not scarce. They're just pretending to be."

Oceane looked at the forty-dollar sign, then at her own empty wallet, then at the line. "So the price should drop when people find out."

It took one weekend. Beatrice came back on Saturday and the display was crowded with pins, the sign now read twelve dollars, and the line had transformed into a loose little cluster of shoppers who strolled up whenever they felt like it. She bought two, one for herself and one for Oceane, and still had money left for a pretzel.

Mr. Pérez, who ran the pretzel stand and lived on her street, leaned on his counter and nodded at her pin. "Nice comet," he said. "You want mustard with that?"

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: A share of stock is a small piece of ownership in a company, so a stockholder owns part of the business and shares in its gains or losses.
story:
Elliot taped the last poster to the front of the table: ELLIOT, MUSA AND JAYCE, LEMONADE, 50 CENTS. The morning was already warm, and the ice in the cooler was crackling as it settled. In his back pocket he kept the envelope his grandfather had given him last night, with a fancy paper inside that said he now owned one share of Fastline Sneakers.

"Does that mean free shoes?" Musa asked, squinting at the paper between customers. Musa wanted new cleats before Saturday's game, and he'd been saving quarters for three weeks, which was why he'd suggested the lemonade stand in the first place.

"Grandpa says no. He says a share of stock is a small piece of ownership in the company. So if I own a share of Fastline, I own part of the business, and I share in its gains or losses." Elliot paraphrased it as best he could, and Jayce frowned like the words had bounced off him.

"Own part of the business," Jayce repeated slowly. He pointed at the lemonade table. "So if somebody buys our stand, and we had shares of it, we'd get some of the money?"

"Basically, yeah."

Ms. Liu from next door crossed the street with her dog, a fat beagle that pulled straight toward the cooler. She paid with a dollar and told them to keep the change. "Are you boys saving up for something?"

"Musa's buying cleats," Elliot said. "I'm trying to figure out this stock thing. Grandpa also mentioned bonds and said one is riskier, and I have to explain which one at dinner Friday, or no dessert."

Ms. Liu laughed. "I'm a bit biased toward bonds myself, at my age, but I'm not telling you the answer. You'll figure it out." She tugged the beagle away from the ice.

Elliot thought about it while he poured cup after cup, the sugar smell mixing with the hot sidewalk and the sticky ring the pitcher left on the table. He set one cup aside for Musa's little sister, who watched them from her bike every day without ever crossing the street. Then he got an idea. "Okay," he said, turning the paper over and drawing with a pencil. "Say we let people buy shares of our stand. Anyone who owns one gets part of whatever we make. If we sell a hundred cups, they win. If it rains all day and we sell three, they lose. Their money goes up and down with us." He drew a second thing. "But a bond is different. It's just lending money, and the borrower pays it back the same no matter what happens to us. If it rains, the lender still gets paid."

Jayce grabbed the pencil. "So the stock people lose if we lose. The bond people don't. That means stock is riskier." He held up the drawing. "Say that at dinner. Grandpa will think we're a whole dynasty of money people."

"A dynasty of one share," Elliot said, and slid the extra cup across the table toward Musa's sister, who finally wheeled her bike over to claim it.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The word "propaganda" comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622.
story:
Gavin boarded the 42 bus with his vocabulary sheet crumpled in his pocket, hunting for a seat. The assignment was due first period: look up the history of one word, write where it came from. He had picked "propaganda" at random, mostly because it sounded cool, and he still had nothing written down. Across from him, Kayden was already glued to a flyer someone in a bright vest had handed out at the stop, the paper still warm from the stack.

"Everybody's signing this," Kayden said, waving it. "The whole school, probably. You don't want to be the only one left out." Above their heads, an ad showed a basketball player Gavin recognized from TV holding a bottle of sports drink, grinning like the drink had personally saved his life. Next to it, a poster warned about a "disgusting, dangerous" new city tax in giant red letters. Three persuasion tricks in one bus, Gavin thought, though he didn't yet have words for the pattern he was noticing.

The man in the vest moved down the aisle, pressing flyers into hands. "Join the movement," he said to each rider. "The smart ones already have." Gavin watched a woman take one without looking, watched two teenagers take two each, watched Kayden nod along. Something about it bothered him, an itch he couldn't scratch. Why did everyone want it more just because everyone else did? He pulled out his phone and typed "propaganda word origin," planning to finish his assignment and maybe illustrate his hunch with the flyer itself.

The screen loaded, and he stopped breathing for a second. He had expected something about politics or war. Instead the entry talked about a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622. The bus made an abrupt turn, and Gavin grabbed the pole to steady himself while the fact sank in. The word wasn't born from dictators or rallies at all. It started with a committee whose whole job was persuading people to believe something.

He leaned over to Kayden, suddenly sure of what he wanted to say. "It's from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide. Pope Gregory XV set it up in 1622."

Kayden blinked. "So it's like church advertising?"

"Kind of. And this guy's doing the same thing." Gavin pointed at the vest, the stack, the grinning faces. "Everyone's taking one because everyone's taking one." Kayden looked down at his own flyer, reread it, then made a quick pivot and dropped it into the recycling bin by the door just as it hissed open at his stop.

"You want the last word for your sheet?" Kayden called from the sidewalk. "It's 'sucker.'"

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a string at its exact midpoint halves the length that vibrates, and the note rises by one octave.
story:
Cameron had borrowed the classroom guitar every lunchtime for two weeks, and his fingertips had gone from sore to tough, like the pads were earning their keep. Today Ms. Leung had asked him to distribute the tuners to everyone before class, small metal clips that hugged the headstock, and Cameron had clipped one to his guitar out of habit.

"It says your E string is flat," said Ria, leaning over from the next chair.

"That's the weird part." Cameron plucked the low string, then pressed down at the twelfth fret, the metal strip almost exactly halfway along the neck. The tuner's needle dropped and shivered. "The tuner says the high one is flat too, but by way more. If they're both E, shouldn't they be wrong by the same amount?"

Ria squinted at the needle. "Maybe you're pressing too hard. Maelle, come look at this."

Maelle crossed the room, still holding her own guitar. "Play the open one." Cameron did. "Now the fret." He did. The two notes rang out, and the second one was unmistakably the same sound, only higher, like the first note's shadow lifted into sunlight.

"They match," Cameron said slowly. "Same note, different height." He measured with his eyes from the nut to the twelfth fret, then from the fret to the bridge. "That's the middle. The string's the same the whole way down, so the only thing I changed was how much of it gets to move." He pressed at the twelfth fret again and watched the length between his finger and the bridge vibrate.

"So when you press the middle," Maelle said, "only half the string is vibrating."

Cameron grabbed a pencil and marked the fret's spot on the whiteboard where Ms. Leung let them sketch ideas. Then he tried pressing at other spots, comparing notes, hunting for the pattern. Ria kept tally marks of which pairs matched and which didn't, like they were working out the probability of a repeat, though Cameron suspected the answer was always going to be the same.

The door opened and Ms. Leung came in carrying a stack of sheet music. She stopped at the whiteboard, where Cameron had written "half = higher" beside his pencil mark.

"Twelfth fret," Cameron said, holding up the guitar. "Want to hear it?"

She set down the stack. "Play it twice."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: In a healthy onion cell, the cell membrane is pressed tightly against the inside of the cell wall, which makes the membrane very hard to see as a separate line.
story:
Connor had been staring into the microscope for so long that his eye ached. The onion skin cells lay before him like pale bricks in a wall, each one neatly outlined. On his worksheet, three labels waited: cell wall, nucleus, and cell membrane. The wall was obvious, the dark dot of the nucleus was easy, but the membrane was nowhere. "Do you see two lines around your cells?" he asked Ria, who was bent over the microscope beside him.

"Two lines?" Ria squinted. "I only see one dark line around each cell. Maybe you forgot to focus." Connor turned the fine adjustment knob slowly, first one way, then the other. The single line around each cell sharpened and blurred, but it never split into two. "Maybe onion cells just don't have a membrane," he said, half hoping she would argue. Ria only shrugged, indifferent to the fate of his worksheet. Behind them, Kylan was already drawing his cells with confident labels, which made it worse.

Connor tried to formulate his problem in words he could test. If the cell wall was the dark outside line, and the membrane was a second line just inside it, then in a healthy cell the two might be squeezed so close together that they looked like one. He remembered the jar of salty water on the supply table at the front of the lab room in the museum's Discovery Hall. Salt water made plants wilt. What would it do to a single layer of onion skin? There was one way to find out.

He walked to the table, took a dropper, and carried it back like it was something precious. "I'm going to put a drop of this on my slide," he told Ria. "If the membrane is stuck against the wall, maybe I can make it come loose." He lowered the drop carefully at the edge of the coverslip and watched through the eyepiece. For a moment nothing changed. Then, cell by cell, something began to peel away from the inside of each dark outline. A thin, faint line pulled inward, shrinking away from the wall like a balloon deflating inside a box.

"There it is!" Connor said. "The cell membrane. It was pressed right up against the wall the whole time, so I couldn't see it as a separate line until now." Ria leaned over to look at his slide and gasped. Ms. Choi, walking past their table, glanced down at his worksheet, where he had written "cell membrane" with an arrow to the shrinking line, and gave him a small nod of approval. When she offered a gentle critique of his drawing and suggested he label the wall as the outer line, not the inner one, Connor just grinned and picked up his pencil. "Kylan," he called across the room, "come look at this. Yours is wrong too."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Universal indicator changes to a range of different colours, and each colour matches a different pH number on a chart.
story:
Michael had the kitchen table to himself until Zayne and Zack arrived, still arguing about whose turn it had been to carry the poster board. He let them argue for a minute, then mediated the only way that ever worked: he put a bowl of chips between them and started laying out his supplies. Litmus paper, a chart he had copied from the library book, a bottle of vinegar, baking soda mixed with water, and, at the far end where his little sister couldn't reach, the drain cleaner his mom had warned him was corrosive.

"Science fair is Saturday," Zayne said, dipping a strip of litmus into the vinegar. It turned pink. "See? Acid. Done."

"That's the problem," Michael said. "It's not done." The rubric Ms. Brown had handed out asked for the pH of each solution, an actual number, and litmus had no numbers in it. It only said acid or base, pink or blue, yes or no. He stared at the pink strip and wondered how you could get a number out of something that only knew two answers. Maybe there was a paper out there that knew more.

Zack flipped through the library book while chewing. "Hey, listen to this." He held it up like he was reading a poem aloud. "Universal indicator changes to a range of different colours, and each colour matches a different pH number on a chart." He turned the book around to show them: a row of colours from red through green to purple, each one sitting above a number.

Michael was already pulling the small bottle from the bottom of his bag. He'd bought it at the hobby shop on Tuesday, on a hunch, without really knowing what it was for. He dropped three drops into the vinegar. The liquid bloomed red, then settled to a deep orange, and when he held it against the chart, it lined up under the number three. Three. Not just acid, but how much acid. He grinned so hard his cheeks hurt.

They tested everything after that. Baking soda water went blue-purple, way up the chart. The drain cleaner went purple, so far to the base end that Michael made Zack hold the chart next to it twice, because it seemed strange that something labeled corrosive could sit on the same scale as soap. Zayne tested lemonade just to see where it landed, and Michael found himself wondering what invisible thing in each liquid made the colours land where they did, like the indicator was translating something he couldn't see.

On Saturday, Ms. Brown stopped at their table, leaned over the row of coloured cups, and asked how they'd chosen their method. Michael held up the chart and the little bottle. "Universal indicator," he said. "Every colour is a different pH."

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: An assist is credited to a player whose pass leads directly to a teammate's basket.
story:
The city had painted a half court onto the asphalt behind the baseball diamond, close enough that a foul ball once dented the backboard, and that was where Felix spent his Saturdays. He was the smallest kid out of the nine who showed up, so Angelo had handed him the ball on the first Saturday and said, "You're the point guard. Boss us around." Felix had not bossed anybody around yet. Today he intended to.

The problem was Alex, who guarded him like Alex was being paid by a corporation that docked his wages for every basket Felix scored. Felix could not get past him. Twice he tried, and twice the ball got swatted into the grass near the pitcher's mound.

He stood at the top of the key and thought about it. Alex stuck to Felix the way a shadow sticks to a shoe. That was the pattern. So maybe the pattern could be used. If Felix ran toward Angelo's defender, that defender would have to step toward Felix, and Alex would follow, and then Angelo would be alone for a second. Felix could not see the second before it happened. He would have to trust it was there.

"Angelo," he called. "Set a screen. Then roll to the hoop." Angelo looked at him, shrugged, and planted himself like a fence post. Felix dribbled off him, and just as Alex and Angelo's defender collided in a tangle of elbows, Felix flicked the pass behind his back. Angelo caught it and laid it in. The net did not even make a sound, it was that clean.

They ran it five more times. It worked four. Ms. Yang, who walked her dog along the outfield fence every Saturday, kept score on a napkin, because she said watching nine kids invent basketball on a baseball diamond was better than television. At the end she read out the totals. Felix had scored two points.

"That can't be right," Alex said. "He ran the whole game."

"He ran the whole game," Ms. Yang agreed, "but an assist is credited to a player whose pass leads directly to a teammate's basket." Angelo, who had scored fourteen, did the arithmetic out loud and found that ten of those baskets had started with Felix's passes. The vote for game MVP was unanimous, all nine kids, even Alex, who raised his hand like it cost him money.

Felix wrote his name and the stat line on the napkin, folded it into his back pocket, and jogged back to the top of the key.

"Same play," he said. "Alex, try to stop it this time."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Prescription flu antiviral medicines work best when started within two days after symptoms begin, which is one reason to see a doctor early.
story:
Elena was still blowing her nose every ten minutes on Thursday when her mother came down with the fever instead. By afternoon, Mom was shivering under two blankets and insisting she would be fine by the weekend. "It's only Thursday," she said. "If I'm not better by Saturday, I'll call the doctor then." Elena sat on the edge of the bed and thought about that. Two days. She remembered the nurse at her own doctor visit saying that the prescription antiviral medicines work best when you start them within two days after symptoms begin, and that this was exactly why you should see a doctor early rather than waiting. If Mom waited until Saturday, she would be right at the edge of that window, or past it.

"Mom, I don't think we should wait," Elena said. "If you go today, they can still give you something that works." Mom groaned, but she let Elena dial the clinic. The receptionist found a slot at five o'clock, and by six Elena was standing at the pharmacy counter with a folded prescription slip, waiting while Ms. Ahmed, the pharmacist who lived on their street, typed at her screen.

"Antiviral," Ms. Ahmed said, reading the slip. "Good timing. Your mom went in quickly?" Elena nodded and explained about the fever starting that morning, and how she had counted the hours on her fingers at home. Ms. Ahmed smiled. "Smart. You caught it in the window." Elena wanted to elaborate, to describe the whole argument she had made in the bedroom, but a line of customers was forming behind her, so she just paid and stepped aside.

Junior was at the magazine rack, supposedly buying cough drops for his grandmother. "Did it work?" he whispered. "Did you actually convince your mom?" "I did math about invisible things," Elena said, feeling pleased. "Like a detective." She peered at the label on the box while they waited for the bus, wondering how anyone had figured out that timing mattered in the first place. Scientists must have watched thousands of patients, she thought, comparing the ones who started early with the ones who started late, until the pattern showed up like footprints in snow.

At home, Mom took the first pill with ginger ale and slept. The next morning her fever had dropped a little, and by Sunday the improvement was gradual but real: she ate toast, then soup, then asked for the crossword. Elena brought her tea and set it on the nightstand. Mom looked up over the rim of her glasses. "Remind me to listen to you sooner next time." "Remind yourself," Elena said. "Two days. That's all you get."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: A small amount of stress before a test or a game can sharpen focus; stress becomes harmful mainly when it lasts for a long time without relief.
story:
Sophia sat at the kitchen table with her kickboard bag packed for tomorrow's swim meet, staring at the same math page she'd read four times. Her heart kept doing a quick double beat, like a conductor rushing the tempo, and her shoulders had crept up toward her ears without asking permission. She noticed the diagonal crease she'd pressed into the paper from reading it so hard, and she wrote at the top of her notebook: Stressed? Since when?

She decided to test it like a science problem. Jitters before a race, she knew, showed up the day of the race and left after. This feeling had come every night for two weeks, ever since she'd started staying up until midnight studying. She tried the breathing exercise the school nurse had shown her class: slow breath in for four counts, out for six, ten times. On the seventh breath her shoulders dropped on their own. It was like finding a switch that governed the whole humming machine of her body. Then she set a real bedtime, ten o'clock, no screens after nine, and wrote it on the fridge where her dad would see it and hold her to it.

That night a message lit up her phone from Yasmine. "Can I ask you something weird? I've felt sick to my stomach every morning for like three weeks. Not just before tests. All the time. Did breathing stuff help you?"

Sophia sat cross-legged on her bed and thought carefully before typing, because she didn't want to get this wrong. "Breathing helps me a lot. But here's the thing I figured out. Some nerves before a race or a test are normal, they can even make you sharper. It's when the stress stays for weeks without letting up that it's a different problem. Three weeks sounds like the second kind. You should talk to someone about it, like your mom or the nurse."

"Three weeks is the bad kind?" Yasmine typed back. "I thought I was just being dramatic."

"You're not dramatic. Promise?"

"Promise. I'll talk to my mom in the morning."

Sophia plugged her phone in across the room, did her slow breathing until her eyelids felt heavy, and slept until the alarm.

At breakfast her dad slid a note across the table, folded in half. "This came for you yesterday. I forgot." It was from Mr. Bui, her swim coach, written in his tidy printing: "Sophia, you've seemed worn down at practice. I moved you to the second heat so you can swim fresh. Just do your best and enjoy it." She read it twice and laughed, because she'd spent two weeks worrying her tiredness would get her cut from the team, and he'd been quietly watching out for her the whole time.

She stuffed the note in her bag, grabbed her kickboard, and called through the house, "Dad, can we leave five minutes early? I want to warm up slow."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: German has one word, "Geschwister," for brothers and sisters together, the way English uses "siblings."
story:
Sawyer slid into the booth at Rosa's Kitchen with his German binder open on his lap. Across the table, Laurel was already eating fries, and Alessandro was balancing a saltshaker on one finger. Mr. Clarke, their neighbour, had promised to quiz them over dinner before Friday's speaking test.

"Ich habe einen Bruder," Sawyer said. "I have one brother. Then I have another brother. And another. And a fourth one." He counted on his fingers. "Plus a sister. In German I have to list all five every time."

"Then your whole turn will be you saying brothers and brothers and brothers," Laurel said.

Mr. Clarke raised an eyebrow but kept stirring his coffee.

Sawyer stared at his notes. Three lines just for siblings, and he still had to describe the dog, the cat, and the rabbit his brother Marco kept in a shoebox. He wondered whether German, which glued words together like "Handschuh" for glove, might have glued something for this too. There had to be a shorter way, and if there was, it would follow the pattern. He texted his cousin in Munich, then set the phone face-up while the waiter brought the pasta.

"Test me while we wait," he told Laurel. She asked about his pets, and he tried "Ich habe einen Hund" until it came out smooth. Alessandro kept dropping the saltshaker and picking it up again, claiming it made his hands agile for the writing section, whatever that meant.

The phone buzzed. Sawyer read the message twice, then grinned. He turned the screen so the others could see it.

"Geschwister," he read. "It means brothers and sisters together, the way English says siblings." He wrote it at the top of his page and underlined it. "One word for all five of them. Ich habe fünf Geschwister."

"That's it? One word?" Alessandro leaned over. "So on Friday you finish your family part in one sentence and get to the dog faster."

"And while you two are still listing," Laurel said, jabbing a fry at them, "I'll have a monopoly on the bonus points."

Mr. Clarke paid the check and gathered his jacket. Sawyer read his new sentence out loud one more time, quietly, under the noise of the restaurant.

"Ich habe fünf Geschwister," he said, and closed the binder.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Endowing means giving your partner a role or trait through what you say, as in 'Doctor, my arm hurts', which makes them the doctor.
story:
Ariana stood in the wings of the community theatre, holding a folded note from Drake. "I freeze every time," he had written. "Nobody gives me anything to be. If I blank out today, cover for me." She tucked the note in her pocket as Mr. He clapped his hands and called the next pair to the stage.

The rule of the afternoon was simple. Whatever your partner said, you answered with yes, and, then added something new. Ariana had liked the idea on paper, but on stage it felt like walking in the dark. When Dana stepped out across from her and said, "We're on a pirate ship and the wheel is spinning," Ariana's mind went white. She said yes and then nothing, and the scene sagged like a wet tent.

Afterwards she sat on the paint-splattered steps and thought about what had actually happened. Dana's line had not just described a ship. It had quietly made Ariana a sailor, because what else would you be, standing at a spinning wheel? There was a hidden mechanism here, invisible, and she began to test it. In the next practice she told Dana, "Nurse, fetch me the bandages," and watched Dana straighten up at once, suddenly someone with a job, someone with lines to say. Whatever you gave your partner through your words, they became it.

She leaned toward Dana between rounds. "I think it's called endowing," she said quietly. Dana nodded and pointed at the stage, where Drake was shuffling out for his turn.

Drake's partner opened a scene about a broken elevator, and Drake just stood there, blinking, hands loose at his sides. Ariana gripped the note in her pocket. Then she remembered she was supposed to be in this scene too, and she stepped in from the side, straight-backed, and barked, "Captain, the cargo hatch is stuck, and only you can force it open."

Drake's shoulders squared. "Aye," he said, planting his feet. "Stand back, everyone. Yes, and somebody hand me that crowbar." The audience of classmates laughed, and Mr. He smiled and wrote something in his notebook, probably sorting them into some category of "improving." Dana leaned over and whispered that the rescue had been radical, in the best way.

Afterward Drake found Ariana by the costume rack. He started to confide that he had been terrified, but she waved it off and handed him a plastic sword. "Next scene," she said. "You're the captain now. Don't lose the ship."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem.
story:
On the second day of drama camp, Mr. Otieno wrote two words on the whiteboard: YES, AND. He told the circle of campers that their afternoon task was to build a scene with a partner, one line at a time, and that each of them had to accept whatever the other one gave. Then he clapped his hands and sent everyone to the far corner of the gym, near the stacked mats and the basketball hoop with no net.

Emily's partner was Felix-Antoine, who was tall and quick and had already been in two school plays. He started their first attempt by pretending to hold a long rod, casting it out over an invisible lake. Emily, busy deciding what clever thing to say, walked toward him and asked whether he had seen her missing backpack. The scene wobbled and died, like a fish too small to keep. Mr. Otieno, wandering past, only said, "Too bad. That was an offer," and moved on.

Emily stood still and turned the words over. An offer. Felix-Antoine hadn't said anything at all, so it had to be the fishing rod itself, the way he had shown where they were without speaking. She tested the idea in her head. If a place could be an offer, maybe a name could too, or a problem. That would mean every single thing a performer said or did was handing the other person something to use, like passing a ball, and dropping it would eliminate the whole game. She looked over at Aryan and his partner, who were deep in a scene about a haunted bakery, each line adding on to the last, and their laughing sounded contagious, spreading across the gym until even Mr. Otieno grinned.

She went back to Felix-Antoine. "Again," she said.

He picked up the invisible rod and cast it. This time Emily looked at what his hands were telling her. "Yes, and the lake is frozen," she said, "so your line is just sitting on top of the ice." Felix-Antoine's eyes lit up. "Yes, and I've been trying to catch the same fish for three years, because it stole my grandmother's ring." "Yes, and she was the queen of a whole dynasty, so that ring belongs in a museum." They leaned on each other, laughing, and built the scene higher and higher until the fish appeared through the ice wearing the ring like a crown.

When Mr. Otieno called time, he asked each pair to show their favorite moment. Felix-Antoine and Emily walked to the middle of the circle, and he cast the invisible line one more time. Emily crouched, peered down at the floor, and said, "Yes, and he's waving at us."
